title: Spin-polarized electron transport for the altermagnet CrSb
authors: V. D. Esin, D. Yu. Kazmin, A. V. Timonina, N. N. Kolesnikov, E. V. Deviatov
abstract: We experimentally investigate spin-polarized electron transport for the centrosymmetric altermagnet CrSb, which is known to reveal both altermagnetic and topological features. We demonstrate pronounced first-harmonic anomalous and second-harmonic non-linear Hall effects for a single-crystal CrSb flake with ferromagnetic nickel contacts, while both effects can not be seen for the reference samples with non-magnetic gold ones. For the anomalous Hall effect, we demonstrate bow-tie hysteresis loop in Hall voltage, which is usually ascribed to surface spin textures in magnetic materials. The slope of the Hall curve changes a sign for two orientations of the Hall-bar contact configuration for the same sample, i.e. for the same sign of the charge carriers. We interpret the observed sign inversion and bow-tie hysteresis as the joint effect of the alternating bulk spin splitting and spin-polarized topological surface states in CrSb. The pronounced non-linear Hall effect with hysteresis in magnetic field confirms finite Berry curvature dipole under injection of spin-polarized electrons, i.e. the topological features for the altermagnetic candidate CrSb.
summary: This work experimentally investigates spin-polarized electron transport in the altermagnet CrSb by measuring anomalous and non-linear Hall effects. By comparing results from ferromagnetic versus non-magnetic contacts, the authors confirm that these unique signatures require spin polarization. The findings strongly suggest that the interplay between bulk magnetism and topological surface states dictates the material's electronic response.
main_problem: To experimentally investigate spin-polarized electron transport, specifically observing anomalous and non-linear Hall effects, in the centrosymmetric altermagnet CrSb.
main_result: Pronounced AHE and NLHE were observed using ferromagnetic Ni contacts, which are absent with non-magnetic Au contacts. The results suggest these effects arise from the joint influence of bulk spin splitting and topological surface states.
method: Transport measurements were performed on single-crystal CrSb flakes at very low temperatures (30 mK) by measuring transverse Hall voltages using both first ($	ext{V}_{1\omega}^{xy}$) and second ($	ext{V}_{2\omega}^{xy}$) harmonic lock-in techniques.
model_or_system: The physical system is the altermagnet CrSb, which is studied as a single crystal flake. The experiment compares measurements using ferromagnetic Ni contacts (inducing spin polarization) against non-magnetic Au reference contacts.
key_observables: Anomalous Hall Effect (AHE) hysteresis loops, sign inversion of AHE slope, and Non-linear Hall Effect ($	ext{V}_{2\omega}^{xy}$) with magnetic field dependence.
important_parameters: Low temperature ($T = 30 	ext{ mK}$), applied magnetic field ($	ext{B}$), and the nature of the contacts (ferromagnetic vs. non-magnetic).
main_assumptions: The observed effects are attributed to spin-polarized current injection from the ferromagnetic Ni contacts, and the geometry is designed to exclude thermoelectric contributions.
figures_summary: Figures show AHE hysteresis loops ($	ext{V}_{1\omega}^{xy}(	ext{B})$) comparing CrSb with Ni leads versus reference samples with Au leads. Another figure compares NLHE signals ($	ext{V}_{2\omega}^{xy} \sim I^2$) for both contact types.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by presenting the experimental setup and measurements, demonstrating the distinct signatures (AHE/NLHE) when using spin-polarized contacts versus non-magnetic controls. The interpretation then links these unique transport features to the theoretical concepts of altermagnetism and topological surface states.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter magnetism/topology, the study's reliance on measuring quantized responses (like harmonic generation) under controlled spin injection provides a highly sensitive probe into electronic band structure symmetries relevant to advanced quantum materials research.
